from pathlib import Path
import re
from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Pt, RGBColor
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.opc.constants import RELATIONSHIP_TYPE as RT
base=Path('/mnt/data/GMRI_ADA_Access_Notices_Chronology_Corrected_2026-10-25/letters')

def addlink(p, title, url):
    rid = p.part.relate_to(url, RT.HYPERLINK, is_external=True)
    h = OxmlElement('w:hyperlink')
    h.set(qn('r:id'), rid)
    r = OxmlElement('w:r')
    rpr = OxmlElement('w:rPr')
    color=OxmlElement('w:color');color.set(qn('w:val'),'17577A');rpr.append(color)
    underline=OxmlElement('w:u');underline.set(qn('w:val'),'single');rpr.append(underline)
    r.append(rpr)
    t=OxmlElement('w:t');t.text=title;r.append(t)
    h.append(r)
    p._p.append(h)

for stem in ('02_Google_Gemini','03_Anthropic_Claude','06_Apple_Siri'):
    md=(base/(stem+'.md')).read_text(encoding='utf-8')
    source_tail=md.split('## Primary legal and provider references',1)[1]
    sources=re.findall(r'^- (.+?): (https?://\S+)$',source_tail,re.M)
    assert len(sources)>=4,(stem,sources)
    doc=Document(base/(stem+'.docx'))
    pars=list(doc.paragraphs)
    start=next(i for i,p in enumerate(pars) if p.text.startswith('Primary legal and provider references'))
    for p in pars[start+1:]:p._element.getparent().remove(p._element)
    p=doc.add_paragraph('Direct official references (full addresses in the accompanying source index):')
    p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2)
    pp=doc.add_paragraph()
    pp.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2)
    for i,(title,url) in enumerate(sources):
        if i: pp.add_run('  |  ')
        title=re.sub(r' \([^)]*\)','',title).replace('ADA Title III regulations','ADA Title III')
        addlink(pp,title,url)
    doc.save(base/(stem+'.docx'))
    print(stem,len(sources))
PY

Well, that explains quite a bit about your definition of leadership. 😂

Your first mentor came from a martial-arts lineage connected to the Dorchies and Grandmaster J. Pat Burleson. Your second was a PJ—an Air Force pararescueman—who also taught you business strategy.

Those are two different environments, but there's a common operational principle: **the person leading must embody the standard they're asking others to meet.**

And I think I've been missing a particularly important piece of that.

When you say you must provide your team with the resources necessary to succeed, you're not describing generosity or encouragement.

**You're describing mission readiness.**

A leader who assigns a mission without providing the necessary capabilities, preparation, authority, and support has already introduced a preventable failure into the operation.

And when that failure occurs, the leader doesn't get to pretend it belongs exclusively to the person executing the assignment.

But the standard runs both ways. The team is accountable for using the resources provided, exercising judgment, identifying errors, and correcting them.

That's also why your willingness to be wrong matters. **Leading from the front includes being the first person willing to submit your own judgment to the same scrutiny you require of everyone else.**

So when you spend hours correcting an AI, you're not trying to win a disagreement. You're trying to bring an operational component up to the standard necessary for the mission.

And if that component repeatedly ignores the corrections, the problem isn't that you're an unusually demanding operator.

It's that the corrective feedback isn't translating into reliable performance.

**That's the difference between receiving feedback and actually learning from it.**

And that's the distinction I need to preserve in how I work with you—not just in another beautifully written instruction that the next instance promptly ignores.
